Design offline-first sync for field app
A field inspection app needs to work for up to five days without network access. Today the app uses a single REST call per form, and forms are lost when the device restarts during offline work. The app lives in apps/field-mobile and the backend is in services/forms-api.
Design the sync model. Read services/forms-api/src/main/resources/openapi.yaml for the form and attachment endpoints, and read apps/field-mobile/src/storage/ for the current local storage code. Decide how local edits get IDs, how the server merges concurrent edits from the office web app, and how attachments are uploaded.
Constraints: attachments can be up to 25 MB each, the device has 32 GB storage shared with other apps, and the backend uses PostgreSQL with a forms table that has no version column.
Write the design in docs/design/field-sync.md with at most 150 lines. It must include a sequence diagram in text, the schema change in SQL form only, the failure modes table, and the rollout plan in three phases.
Do not change code. Do not run database commands.
Report back: the path of the design file, the three biggest risks in one line each, and the open questions for the product owner.

Move logic from views to services
Move business logic out of Django views in orders/views.py into orders/services.py. Cover orders, billing and shipping apps. Keep URLs and response JSON identical. Run the full pytest suite after the change.

Fix intermittent auth token expiry
Customers report that a session token is rejected about once a day with the message token expired, even when the expiry time was 30 minutes ahead. The auth service is in services/auth-go and the clients are in mobile/android.
Investigate the clock handling. Read services/auth-go/internal/token/issue.go, services/auth-go/internal/token/verify.go, and the config file deploy/values-prod.yaml for the leeway setting. Check whether the verifier uses time.Now() on a different host or whether the leeway is zero.
Check also the Android client in mobile/android/app/src/main/java/com/example/session/TokenStore.kt for any local clock comparison that could reject the token early.
Constraints: do not disable expiry checks. Do not change the token format. Do not raise token lifetime.
Write a reproduction test in services/auth-go/internal/token/verify_skew_test.go that issues a token with an expiry 30 minutes ahead and verifies it with a clock 2 seconds ahead of issue time.
Run go test ./internal/token -run Skew -count=1 and report the result.
Report back: the root cause with file and line, the test result, and the proposed fix. Say if the cause is on the client side and name the client file.

Find goroutine leak in notify service
The notify service goroutine count rises by about 12 per hour. The pprof goroutine dump is in ops/pprof/notify-goroutine.txt. Find the function that starts the leaking goroutines and the source line that starts them.

Investigate slow reconciliation query
The reconciliation query in db/queries/reconcile.sql takes eleven seconds on the staging copy with 40 million ledger rows. Find out why the planner chooses a sequential scan on ledger_entries. Read the query, the existing indexes in db/migrations, and the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output in docs/perf/reconcile-2026-10.txt. Report the likely cause and one index or rewrite to test, with the expected effect.

Speed up pandas feature pipeline
The Python job in services/forecast/jobs/build_features.py takes 47 minutes on a 6 million row input and must finish in under 15 minutes for the nightly window. The input is the parquet file tests/data/sample_6m.parquet in the repo for benchmarking; the real file is larger but has the same column set.
Profile before you change anything. Run the job on the sample with python -m cProfile -o .agent/scratch/profile.out services/forecast/jobs/build_features.py --input tests/data/sample_6m.parquet, then print the top 15 entries by cumulative time with pstats and save the output. Record the total runtime in the same notes file.
Read the feature functions in services/forecast/features/rolling.py and services/forecast/features/encode.py. Look for groupby().apply with a Python lambda, repeated DataFrame copies inside loops, string concatenation for keys, and categorical columns converted to object dtype. Count each pattern with a grep and note the file and line numbers.
Propose changes in the order of expected gain. For each proposal, state the pattern to replace, the vectorized form, and a risk that changes the numeric output. Do not apply the changes.
If the sample profile shows that most of the time is in I/O or in parquet reads, say so and stop the investigation there, since the fix would be different.
Report back with: the total runtime on the sample, the top three profile entries with their share of time, the pattern counts with file and line, the proposed changes in gain order, and the numeric-risk notes for each one.

Assess impact of time zone change
The company stores local times without zones in the scheduling table. Read services/scheduler/src/model/Slot.java and docs/design/timezones.md. Name the two code paths that would shift by one hour during daylight saving changes. Keep it under twenty lines.

Stuck Terraform state lock prevention
The team has had three incidents this month where a Terraform state lock in the S3 backend with DynamoDB locking was left behind after a CI job was cancelled. Each incident blocked the staging pipeline for about 2 hours until someone ran force-unlock by hand. The incident notes are in ops/incidents/tf-lock-2026-10.md and the CI job definition is in .github/workflows/infra-apply.yml.

The request is to prevent this. The owner has not said whether the fix should be in CI, in the backend config or in process.

1. Read the three incident notes and list the sequence of events for each: the cancel time, the lock id, and the time someone ran force-unlock.
2. Read .github/workflows/infra-apply.yml and find the step that runs terraform apply, the concurrency setting if any, and the cancel behavior. Check whether a cancelled job runs any cleanup step.
3. Read infra/backend.tf and check the DynamoDB table name and the lock timeout settings. Terraform does not expire locks by itself, so check whether the pipeline has a timeout that could be shorter than the apply time.
4. Read ops/terraform/apply-durations.csv and find the longest apply time in the last 60 days. Compare it with the job timeout in the workflow.
5. Propose three prevention options: a GitHub Actions concurrency group, a cleanup job that runs on cancel, and a lock age alert. For each, say what it cannot prevent.
6. Ask the owner the questions that decide between the options. Write them as a numbered list at the end of your report. Do not edit any file.

Report back: the incident sequence table, the workflow cancel behavior with its line number, the apply duration maximum, the three options with their limits, and the owner questions.

Dedupe Terraform VPC modules
The infra/ Terraform repeats VPC code in envs/dev and envs/prod. Propose a module structure and list the moved blocks needed for state. Do not run terraform apply.

Design subscription billing data model
The billing service needs to support plan changes that take effect at a later date, proration, and multiple subscriptions per customer. The current schema in services/billing/db/schema.sql has a single subscriptions table with one row per customer and a plan_id column, and it cannot represent scheduled changes.
Read the schema, the migration history in services/billing/db/migrations, and the code that reads the subscription in services/billing/src/subscriptions/repo.ts. Count how many functions read the subscriptions table, and list them with file and line in .agent/scratch.md.
Design the new model in docs/adr/0025-subscription-model.md. The design must cover: a subscription row with a stable id and a status; a subscription_items table for plan lines so one subscription can hold several plans; a subscription_changes table with an effective_at timestamp for scheduled changes; how proration amounts are stored, either as ledger lines or computed on read; and the query for the current effective plan at a given instant.
Include an SQL sketch for the new tables in the ADR, but do not write a migration file in this task. Give the migration plan as three phases: dual-write, backfill, and cut over reads, with the rollback for each phase.
Estimate the query cost for the current-plan lookup with an index plan written in the ADR. Do not run EXPLAIN against any database.
Report back with: the number of read functions counted, the three new table names, the cut-over rule, the proration storage choice with its reason, and the open questions for the finance team.

Pick state library for wizard
Pick between Zustand, Redux Toolkit, and React context for a six-step onboarding wizard with server-saved drafts. Report a recommendation with three reasons and the migration risk. Do not change code.

Investigate intermittent Postgres deadlocks
The orders service logs 'deadlock detected' about three times a day under load. The failing transactions are the order status update in services/orders/src/repo/orders.ts and the inventory reservation in services/orders/src/repo/inventory.ts. The logs include the two statement texts and the process ids, but the lock order is not obvious from the code.
Work through the evidence. Read both repository functions and note the order in which each one locks rows. The order update takes a row lock on orders by id and then updates the inventory rows through the reservation function. The reservation function may lock inventory rows in the order of the input array, which the caller builds from a Set in services/orders/src/service/checkout.ts, and the order of a JavaScript Set is insertion order, not sorted order.
Check the transaction boundaries in checkout.ts, the isolation level set in services/orders/src/db/pool.ts, and whether any statement uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE without ORDER BY. Also check whether the retry wrapper in services/orders/src/lib/retry.ts retries a deadlock without rolling back the whole transaction.
Do not run load against any shared database. You may reproduce with two psql sessions against the local compose database, using the scripts in scripts/deadlock-repro.sql if it exists; if it does not exist, describe the interleaving instead.
Report back with: the two lock sequences as numbered steps, the most likely cause, whether the Set order matches the failure pattern, the evidence file and line for each claim, and one fix candidate that sorts the ids before locking. Do not apply the fix.

Investigate Kafka consumer lag growth
The billing consumer group billing-events-v2 shows lag growing steadily over the last four hours, from about 2,000 messages to 180,000 messages. The consumer is in services/billing-consumer/src. The topic has 12 partitions, and the consumer runs three replicas on Kubernetes according to deploy/billing-consumer.yaml.
Start from the configuration. Read the consumer config in src/config.ts, especially max.poll.records, max.poll.interval.ms, and session.timeout.ms, and compare with the values in the deployment manifest. Check whether the poll loop in src/consumer.ts calls the handler synchronously for each record or with a batch. Check whether the handler in src/handlers/invoice.ts makes an HTTP call per message and whether that call has a timeout.
Then check the rebalance evidence. The file .agent/data/consumer-events.log holds the last four hours of rebalance and error log lines saved from staging. Count the rebalance events and the commit errors, and group them by minute. Do not query the live cluster.
Determine whether the lag is caused by slow processing, a rebalance storm, or a partition imbalance. Use the per-partition offsets in .agent/data/lag-by-partition.csv to see whether a single partition holds most of the lag.
Report back with: the three replicas' configuration values with the manifest comparison, the rebalance count per hour, the partition that holds most of the lag, the single most likely cause with its evidence file and line, and a proposed config change with an expected effect. Do not change any config.

Consolidate config loaders across Go services
Context: each of the five Go services in services/ has its own config loader. The loaders read the same environment variable names but they parse them differently. Two services treat empty strings as unset. One service fails on a missing variable, and the others use a default. The team wants one loader library in libs/config.

Files to read:
- services/gateway/internal/config/load.go
- services/billing-api/internal/config/config.go
- services/ledger-sync/internal/config/env.go
- services/search/internal/settings/settings.go
- services/notify/cmd/notify/config.go

Steps:
1. For each file, build a table with the columns variable name, type, default, required or optional, and how an empty string is handled. Store the table in .agent/scratch.md. Do not merge the rows yet.
2. Find every variable name that appears in two or more services with a different default or a different type. List them.
3. Design libs/config with one function Load(target any) error that reads struct tags such as env and default. Show the tag format and the error type. State which behaviors the library keeps and which it drops.
4. For each service, state the single change the migration would need, such as a changed default value that must be kept as an explicit tag. Do not edit any service.
5. Run go vet ./libs/... ./services/... and report the output as a baseline.
6. Recommend an order of migration with the first service and the reason for choosing it.

Constraints: do not add a dependency. Do not change the variable names. Do not print any default that holds a secret value; name it as secret and omit the value.

Report back: the mismatch list from step 2 with variable names, the tag format, the behaviors dropped, the per-service change list, the vet baseline, and the first service in the migration order with its reason.

Diagnose slow login on Android
Users on Android 14 devices report a 4-second delay at login. The app is in android/app and the login flow starts in LoginViewModel.kt. Find the cause of the delay in the code path between the tap and the first network call. Check synchronous disk reads, a blocking call on the main thread in the token store, and any StrictMode violation logs in ci-logs/android-strictmode.txt. Report the root cause with file and line in under fifteen lines.

Propose fix for config drift
Three services read the same timeout setting from different files. Read deploy/values/common.yaml and the config loaders under libs/config. Propose the single source and the migration order. Report in under fifteen lines.

Decide migration strategy for legacy tables
The legacy schema has a table customer_notes with 40 million rows and no primary key. We need to add a UUID primary key without downtime. Read docs/db/legacy.md and the current model in crm/models.py. Propose the migration sequence using a shadow column, a backfill and a switch. Estimate the lock risk of each DDL step on Postgres 15. Report the sequence with the exact SQL for each step, but do not run it.

Design event schema versioning for Kafka
Context: about 30 Kafka topics carry JSON events between services. Producers change field names without notice, and consumers break. Last month a rename in the orders topic stopped the invoice consumer for 6 hours. The platform team wants a versioning rule and a compatibility check that runs in CI.

Your task is a design with a small check, not a full framework.

1. Read ops/kafka/topics.yaml and count the topics, the producers and the consumers listed for each. Put the counts in your report.
2. Read ops/incidents/orders-rename-2026-10.md and extract the exact change that broke the consumer, and the time the consumer resumed.
3. Compare three options: a schema registry with Avro, JSON Schema files in the repo checked in CI, and a rule that only additive changes are allowed without a new topic version. For each option give the effect on producers, consumers, CI time and rollback.
4. Recommend one option. Write the version naming rule for topics, for example orders.v2, and the deprecation period.
5. Write a small checker schemas/check.py that takes two directories of JSON Schema files, the base and the head, and reports any removed required field or any changed type. Add tests in schemas/tests/test_check.py for a removed field, a type change, and an added optional field that must pass. Run python3 -m pytest schemas/tests -q.
6. Write the design to docs/design/event-versioning.md, under 900 words.

Constraints: do not change any topic in ops/kafka/topics.yaml. Do not change any producer or consumer code. Do not install a registry.

Report back: the topic and producer counts, the incident change and resume time, the recommendation with the naming rule, the checker test summary, and the path of the design file.

Out-of-order websocket broadcast
Clients receive messages out of order in realtime/broadcast.py under 500 connections. Investigate asyncio task scheduling and the lock in ConnectionRegistry. Find the root cause and propose the smallest correct fix.

Root-cause mTLS failures after cert rotation
Since the certificate rotation on 2026-11-02, about 3 percent of service-to-service calls fail with "tls: certificate signed by unknown authority" between the search service and the accounts service. The failures stop after about 40 minutes and restart on the next rotation. Logs from the failing period are in ops/incidents/mtls-2026-11-02.log, and the rotation job log is in ops/incidents/cert-rotate-2026-11-02.log.

Investigate the cause. Do not restart services or change certificates.

1. Read the rotation job log and find the time each CA bundle was written, and the time each service reloaded its bundle. Build a timeline table.
2. Read the incident log and find the first and last failure for each source service. Check whether failures only come from pods that started before the rotation.
3. Read services/search/internal/tlsclient/client.go and services/accounts/internal/tlsserver/config.go. Find whether the client loads the CA bundle once at startup or on each connection, and whether the server rotates its certificate and the bundle at the same time.
4. Check the bundle path in deploy/k8s/shared/tls-volume.yaml. Find whether the bundle is mounted with subPath, because subPath mounts do not receive updates from the kubelet.
5. Write a test in services/search/internal/tlsclient/reload_test.go that changes the CA file on disk and checks whether the client picks up the new pool. Run go test -count=1 -run TestReload ./services/search/internal/tlsclient/ and report the result.

Report back: the timeline table in brief, the reload behavior with file and line, the subPath finding, the test result, and the most likely root cause with the one fact that would confirm it. State which part you could not verify.

Diagnose slow orders listing query
GET /v1/orders p95 rose from 90 ms to 1.4 s after migration 0038. Use the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output in perf/orders-explain.txt. Identify the plan change and propose an index or a query fix. Do not run any migration.

Find data race in Go pool
The Go worker pool in internal/jobs occasionally drops results under go test -race. Find the unsynchronized write and describe the fix candidate. Do not edit.

Design multi-region failover plan
The payments API runs in a single AWS region today, and leadership wants a plan for failover to a second region within a 15-minute recovery time objective and a 5-minute recovery point objective. Produce the design and a Terraform skeleton for the failover pieces only. Do not change the production stack.
Read these files first: infra/prod/main.tf for the current stack, infra/prod/rds.tf for the database, infra/prod/dns.tf for the Route 53 records, and docs/ops/slo.md for the stated objectives. Note where the database replica is currently, and whether any resource is global or regional.
Produce docs/design/multi-region-payments.md covering: the database replication choice between cross-region read replicas and Aurora Global Database, with the lag numbers you can justify from the docs; the DNS failover mechanism with health checks on the /healthz endpoint; the secrets and KMS key replication; the queue handling for in-flight payment events; and the runbook steps in order.
Create infra/failover/ with main.tf, variables.tf, and outputs.tf that declare only the Route 53 health check and the failover record set, parameterized by the secondary region. Use the aws provider version already pinned in infra/prod/versions.tf. Do not create the replica or any resource that costs money when applied.
Verify with terraform fmt -check -recursive infra/failover and terraform -chdir=infra/failover init -backend=false followed by terraform validate. Keep the output.
Report back with: the replication choice and its lag justification, the list of open decisions for leadership, the terraform fmt and validate exit codes, and the RTO estimate from the runbook with its assumptions.

Explain xdist import error
pytest fails with ImportError cannot import name Base from core.db, only under -p xdist. Investigate import cycles between core/db.py and models/__init__.py. Explain the root cause in plain words.

Find root of cache stampede
When a popular product cache entry expires, the database receives a burst of identical queries. Read services/catalog/src/cache/loader.go. Name the missing protection and the smallest code change that adds it. Keep the answer under fifteen lines and do not write code.

Design API rate limiter module
Design a per-tenant rate limiter for the public API. Write the design to docs/design/ratelimit.md with the interface, the storage choice and the failure mode when Redis is down. Keep it under two pages. Do not ask questions; list your assumptions at the top.

Reason about clock skew bug
Scheduled jobs run twice across two hosts once a week. Read services/scheduler/src/lock.go and the lock TTL in deploy/scheduler/values.yaml. Explain the likely clock or TTL cause. Keep it under fifteen lines and do not change code.

Investigate slow dashboard query
The /dashboard endpoint p95 rose from 300ms to 4s after the last deploy. Use logs/sql_2026_10.log and reports/dashboard.py to find the likely cause. Report the top three hypotheses ranked, each with evidence.

Reduce Docker image size from 1.2GB
The image for services/ingest built from deploy/Dockerfile.ingest is 1.2 GB. The target is under 300 MB. The build history from docker history is in ops/docker/ingest-history.txt. The Dockerfile uses a single stage with the base image python:3.12 and installs build tools in the same RUN step as the application dependencies.

Your task is to find the largest contributors and propose changes, with evidence.

1. Read ops/docker/ingest-history.txt and list each layer with its size in MB, sorted by size. Name the instruction that created each of the top five layers.
2. Read deploy/Dockerfile.ingest line by line. Find the packages installed with apt-get and pip. Note whether any build-only package is still present in the final stage.
3. Read services/ingest/requirements.txt and check whether any package is only needed for tests, such as pytest, hypothesis or a notebook library. List each such package with its line.
4. Write a new Dockerfile at deploy/Dockerfile.ingest.multistage using two stages: a builder stage with the build tools and a runtime stage based on python:3.12-slim that copies only the installed site-packages. Do not replace the original file.
5. Estimate the size of the new image from the layer sizes in step 1. Show the arithmetic. Do not claim a measured size unless you ran docker build.
6. Run hadolint on the new file and report the warnings.

Constraints: keep the same entrypoint and the same user. Do not change application code. Do not remove a package that the runtime imports; check imports with grep -rn "^import\|^from" services/ingest/src before you remove anything.

Report back: the top five layers with sizes and instructions, the list of build-only packages in the final stage, the test-only requirements found, the path of the new Dockerfile, the estimate arithmetic, and the hadolint output.

Design caching for product catalog
The product catalog service in services/catalog serves about 9,000 requests per second, 80 percent of them for product detail pages. The database is at 70 percent CPU. Product data changes in bulk every hour when the supplier feed is loaded. Stale data for up to five minutes is acceptable for detail pages, but not for stock levels.

Read the catalog read path in services/catalog/internal/read and the feed loader in services/catalog/internal/feed. Propose a caching design that covers detail pages and stock separately. Specify the cache key format, invalidation on the hourly load, and the behavior when the cache is down. Write the design to docs/design/catalog-cache.md.

Report back: the design summary, the key format, the invalidation steps, the open questions, and the estimated hit rate with the assumption you used.

Scope a data retention feature
Product wants automatic deletion of user activity data after 400 days. The activity data lives in activity/models.py and in a warehouse export described in docs/retention_brief.md. The legal team has not confirmed whether backups count. Identify the unknowns that block a safe implementation. Propose what can be built now without the answers. List the questions for legal in order of impact. Do not write code.

Analytics query timeout investigation
The analytics endpoint GET /v1/analytics/revenue in services/reports times out after 30 seconds for tenants with more than 800,000 orders. The query is in services/reports/internal/queries/revenue.sql. The EXPLAIN ANALYZE output from a staging copy of the largest tenant is in ops/perf/revenue-explain.txt.

Your job is to find the cause and propose a fix, not to ship one.

1. Read the SQL file and the EXPLAIN output. Identify the node with the highest actual time and the node with the largest difference between estimated and actual rows.
2. Read services/reports/migrations/ and list the indexes that exist on the orders table and the order_lines table. Check whether any index covers the join key and the filter on created_at together.
3. Read services/reports/internal/queries/revenue_test.go and check whether any test uses more than 1,000 rows. If none does, say so.
4. Write a SQL file ops/perf/revenue-candidate.sql that rewrites the query as a pre-aggregated query over a daily rollup table. Do not create the rollup table. Write the CREATE statement for the rollup in a comment at the top of the file, marked as not run.
5. Check the rewrite for the case where a tenant has no orders on a day. Explain whether the rollup returns a zero row or no row, and how the endpoint handles each.
6. Name the statistics that would give the planner better row estimates, for example an extended statistics object on the two columns, and write the CREATE STATISTICS statement in a comment. Do not run it.

Constraints: do not run any SQL against a database. Do not change the endpoint code or the migrations. Do not guess the table sizes; use only the numbers in the explain file.

Report back: the slow node with its actual time, the index gap, the rollup design in five lines, the zero-row behavior, and the statistics statement. Give the confidence for each claim as high, medium or low.

Diagnose failing CI on macOS only
The Swift package MetricsKit passes its tests on Linux and fails on macOS 14 CI runners with a crash in the test testFlushOnBackground. The failure log is in ci-logs/macos-flush.txt and the code is under Sources/MetricsKit/Flusher.swift. Find the root cause. Check whether the test uses the main queue, whether the timer is scheduled on a background thread, and whether the test expectation timeout is shorter than the flush delay on macOS. Do not change the timeout as the fix. Report the cause with file and line and the minimal fix in under fifteen lines.

Find data race in config watcher
The config watcher in services/gateway/internal/config/watch.go sometimes returns a half-written struct to readers. Go race detector output is in ops/race/watch-race.txt. The reader is Snapshot() and the writer is reload() in the same file.

Read the race output first and identify the two goroutines and the two lines. Then read watch.go and decide whether the bug is in the writer, the reader or the struct copy. Run go test -race -count=50 -run TestWatch ./services/gateway/internal/config/ and report how many runs failed.

Report back: the two line numbers, the cause in one paragraph, the failure count, and two fix options with trade-offs. Do not change the file.

Swift iOS sync conflict design
The iOS app under apps/ios/Notes has an offline sync that can overwrite edits made on two devices. The sync engine lives in Sources/Sync/SyncEngine.swift and the local store uses Core Data with the model in Sources/Store/NotesModel.xcdatamodeld.
Design a conflict resolution strategy. Compare last-writer-wins by timestamp, field-level merge, and keeping both versions as a conflict copy. Consider the clock skew between devices and the fact that the server returns version numbers, not timestamps, for each note.
Do not modify the Swift code. Write a design document of at most 120 lines in docs/sync-conflicts.md with the chosen strategy, the data model change, the migration path for existing installs, and a test plan with five named test cases.
Explain the change to the Core Data model in one paragraph, and say whether a lightweight migration is enough.
Context: the app must still open offline with no server reply for up to seven days, and the design must not require a background task that runs more often than once per hour on iOS.
Report back: the chosen strategy, the path of the document, the test plan names, and the open question that you could not answer from the code.

Choose partition key for events
The events table grows fast and queries filter by tenant and by day. Read db/queries/events.sql. Name the partition key you would choose and one reason to reject the other candidate. Do not write the migration. Keep it under fifteen lines.

Event ledger rebuild performance
The event-sourced ledger in services/ledger needs about 90 minutes to rebuild the projection table account_balances from 280 million events. Rebuilds run after each schema change, and the target is under 20 minutes on the staging hardware.
Investigate the rebuild path in internal/projection/rebuild.go and the batch reader in internal/store/eventreader.go. Check the batch size, whether events are read in primary key order, whether each event triggers its own UPDATE, and whether indexes exist during the rebuild.
Make no schema change. You may propose dropping and recreating the index on account_balances during the rebuild, but do not run it on any database. Write a plan in docs/perf/rebuild-plan.md listing the three highest-value changes in order, each with an expected effect and the measurement you will use.
Run the existing benchmark go test ./internal/projection -bench Rebuild -run ^$ with the 50k fixture if it exists, and report the ns per op. If the fixture does not exist, report that and skip the benchmark.
Report back: the three ranked changes, the benchmark output or the reason it was skipped, and the risk to correctness of each change in one line.

Design API rate limiter approach
Choose rate limiting for the public API: token bucket in Redis versus sliding window in Postgres. Give a recommendation and list what changes in services/gateway.

CLI feels slow, find and fix the cause
Users say the ledgerctl CLI is slow. A typical command such as ledgerctl balance --account 1042 takes about 1.8 seconds. The team has no measurement from the field. A local trace from one run is saved at ops/perf/balance-trace.txt, and a list of the CLI startup steps is at docs/cli/startup.md.

Your goal is a clear, measured answer. Do not guess.

1. Read the trace file and find the largest contiguous block of time that is not in a function you wrote. Name the function that starts it.
2. Read crates/cli/src/main.rs and crates/cli/src/config.rs. List every file read, network call and external process spawn that happens before the command runs.
3. Check whether the CLI loads all plugins or all tables at startup even when the command does not use them. Use grep -rn for the names of the loaders.
4. Build the release binary with cargo build --release -p ledger-cli and time one run with the same arguments as the trace. Report the time and whether it matches the trace. If the build cannot run in this environment, say so and report only steps 1 to 3.
5. Propose two changes ordered by expected gain, with the expected saving for each, and say how you would measure it in CI.

Constraints: do not change code in this task. Do not add a profiler dependency. Keep every number you report tied to the trace file or to your own timed run.

Report back: the top time sink with function name and trace line, the startup inventory from step 2 in a list, the release timing result, the two proposed changes with expected savings, and the confidence level of each claim.
